title: Swiss export growth, the franc and the margins beneath the headline
summary: Martin Schlegel’s 3 November presentation in St Gallen starts with a puzzle for an open economy. Switzerland had kept growing through an unsettled international environment. Yet a firm negotiating its next export contract could still be facing a serious currency problem. Slide 3 compares GDP growth with unemployment. The GDP series removes the effect of major sporting events, whose revenues can distort the Swiss quarterly figures. That adjustment matters when using a quarter of national growth to judge how much business local employers are doing.

Goods exports helped explain the resilience. Slides 4–6 trace exports in volume terms and compare the paths for the United States, the European Union and other destinations. Indexing all three to the first quarter of 2022 makes their growth rates comparable. The indices do not give the contribution of each destination to the change in total exports. Calculating that requires the starting shares as well. The industrial breakdown adds another qualification. Pharmaceuticals and chemicals supported growth, alongside other industries, so the aggregate could rise even while particular producers experienced weaker orders.

A similar distinction applies to the currency. Slide 8 compares the franc with a basket of trading partners’ currencies. Since 2020 its nominal index had risen substantially while its real index, adjusted for relative prices, finished much closer to its starting level. If foreign prices rise faster than Swiss prices, a firm can experience appreciation on the foreign-exchange screen with a smaller deterioration in relative prices. The real index is an economy-wide average. A producer buying Swiss inputs and billing an overseas customer in dollars encounters the exchange rate in its cash flow immediately.

The business interviews and invoicing charts show where that difference becomes material. Roughly half of the firms shown on slide 9 reported margin pressure from appreciation. Some reported lower sales, while about one in ten benefited through costs. The presentation puts pharmaceuticals at 47% of export value and machinery, electrical goods and metals together at 24%. A separate chart assigns 42% of export invoicing to francs, 31% to dollars and 25% to euros. These shares describe different dimensions of trade. They cannot tell us the dollar exposure of a pharmaceutical producer without information about that firm’s invoices, input costs and hedges.

The SNB’s regional contacts also contributed a forward-looking measure. Slide 13 asks about expected real sales over the next four quarters. Confidence had picked up from its recent low. An improving balance of replies can coexist with modest output growth, particularly if the firms expecting an improvement have small sales volumes. Slide 14 placed 2026 GDP growth in a 1.5–2% range while anticipating more moderate quarterly growth after the exceptionally strong second quarter. A strong quarter already in the annual arithmetic can lift the year’s average even if the expansion subsequently slows.

Schlegel closed with domestic prices and the September policy assessment. The decomposition on slide 15 assigns much of the recent inflation increase to petroleum products. Slide 16 compares conditional forecasts from March, June and September, each assuming a 0% policy rate. The September projection put annual inflation at 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for each of 2027 and 2028. The chart puts oil-driven inflation today alongside the Bank’s assessment of price pressure several years ahead. The forecast shown at the November event came from the September decision.

questions.question: How could export values look resilient while a manufacturer reports weaker profitability?
questions.detail: Build a bridge from foreign-currency sales to franc cash flow. Separate quantities, invoice prices, exchange rates and imported input costs. A firm with a fixed dollar contract and franc payroll loses revenue in francs as the currency appreciates. A pharmaceutical producer facing relatively stable volumes can dominate the national export series while less diversified suppliers absorb lower margins.

questions.question: Which exchange rate belongs in an analysis of competitiveness?
questions.detail: Match the rate to the question. The real trade-weighted rate compares prices across many destinations. A bilateral nominal rate translates a specific invoice. For a manufacturer that buys components in dollars, exports to the euro area and borrows in francs, trace the currency of each transaction and the timing of the hedge before inferring an earnings effect.

questions.question: What would distinguish a temporary oil shock from broader inflation pressure?
questions.detail: Follow the petroleum contribution together with prices for domestic services and imported goods excluding fuel. If fuel inflation fades while other categories accelerate and business contacts report wider price increases, the case for persistent pressure strengthens. The September projection provides a dated baseline for that comparison. Events between September and the speech are relevant when comparing it with a later price release.

questions.question: Can the survey quantify the GDP benefit of improved business confidence?
questions.detail: The question asks firms about the direction of future sales. To turn that signal into a growth estimate, an analyst would need respondents’ sales weights, the size of each expected change and the historical relationship between replies and realised activity.

limitation: The slides report rounded export shares and survey balances. They give no sector-by-currency cross-tabulation or hedge positions. The 2026 growth range and inflation projections are forecasts available at the dated presentation.
